57.title: Who do you say I am? (Matthew 16:13–20)
57.hook: Peter answers first, and is given a name meaning rock and the keys of the kingdom
57.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Chair of Saint Peter on February 22, and churches East and West keep Saints Peter and Paul on June 29. Many Christians describe coming to faith as answering this question for themselves, and some churches ask it in confirmation or at baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter walks on water: he stepped out, sank, and was caught. Your line was he catches the sinking. What step did you take? Today a new stretch begins: Jerusalem and the last week. Day fifty-seven.

People ask what you do for work, where you're from, what you're into. It's rare that someone asks who you think they are. Now picture the far north of the land, near the springs where the Jordan River begins, at a town called Caesarea Philippi. It was a place full of shrines to other gods, and a city named for Caesar. Jesus and his disciples are walking, and he asks them an easy question first: what are people saying about me? Then a hard one. Today's word: the keys.
screen: `WHO DO YOU THINK THEY ARE?` → `CAESAREA PHILIPPI, FAR NORTH.` → `AN EASY QUESTION, THEN A HARD ONE.`

segments.voice: The easy question, in the King James Bible: "Whom do men say that I the Son of man am?" The answers come quickly. Some say John the Baptist, back from the dead. Some say Elijah. Others, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. Then he turns it: "But whom say ye that I am?" You. Not the crowds. Silence, probably. And then Peter, first as usual: "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God." Christ is the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah: the anointed one, the king God promised. Jesus calls him blessed, and says this didn't come from any human being, but from his Father in heaven. Then he gives Simon a new name: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." There's a pun inside. In Greek, Peter is Petros, and rock is petra. In Aramaic, the language they spoke, it's the same word both times: Kepha, which is why Paul calls him Cephas. Then: "And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Keys meant authority, the steward of a house who opens and shuts the doors. Here Christians read differently, and deeply. Catholics understand the rock as Peter himself, with his authority passed on to the bishops of Rome; the keys appear on the papal coat of arms. Orthodox Christians honor Peter as first among the apostles, and many of their teachers read the rock as Peter's confession of faith, with authority held by the bishops together. Many Protestants read the rock as that confession, or as Christ himself. All of them keep the question at the center: who do you say I am?
screen: `WHOM DO MEN SAY THAT I AM?` · `BUT WHOM SAY YE?` · `PETROS, PETRA, KEPHA.` · `THE KEYS: WHO OPENS AND SHUTS.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably, and let your breathing slow. Now let the question come to you, just as it came to them. Not what your parents said. Not what your church says, or your friends, or the internet. Who do you say he is? A teacher. A prophet. The Christ. A question mark. Someone you're still meeting. There's no wrong answer in the privacy of your own head, and nobody's grading it. Just be honest with yourself. If you pray, you can bring your answer to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
The keys. The authority to open and shut, given to Peter, the rock, after he answered the hard question. Churches read the keys in different ways.
Your line: the question is for you. Today, when someone asks what you think, pause and give your own answer, not the crowd's. Day fifty-seven.

58.title: The mountain of light (Matthew 17:1–8)
58.hook: on a mountain his face shines like the sun, and Peter wants to build tents
58.carry: you can't stay on the mountain
58.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches keep the feast of the Transfiguration on August 6, and many Protestant churches read the story on the Sunday before Lent. On that day many Orthodox churches bless the first fruits of the harvest, often grapes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the keys, and a hard question: who do you say I am? Your line was the question is for you. What did you answer? Six days later, Matthew says, they climb a mountain. Day fifty-eight.

Most people have had a moment or two they can't quite explain. A sunrise that stopped them. A birth. A piece of music. A second when everything seemed lit from the inside, and you wished you could stay there forever. Now picture Jesus taking just three of his friends, Peter, James and John, up a high mountain, away from everyone. Matthew doesn't name the mountain. Tradition says it was Mount Tabor, in Galilee, a round hill rising alone from the plain. And up there, in front of them, something happens that they'll carry for the rest of their lives. Today's word: transfiguration.
screen: `A MOMENT LIT FROM INSIDE.` → `THREE FRIENDS, A HIGH MOUNTAIN.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS.`

segments.voice: Matthew says he was transfigured before them, in the King James Bible: "and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light." The Greek word is metamorphoo, the root of our metamorphosis: changed in form. The Latin became transfiguration. And then two more figures appear, talking with him: Moses, who gave the law, and Elijah, the great prophet. The law and the prophets, the whole story of Israel, on one mountain. Then Peter, and you've got to love Peter, doesn't know what to say, so he says something practical: "Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias." Tabernacles means tents, shelters. Let's build something. Let's stay. While he's still talking, a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says what it said at the river: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him." Hear him. Not build for him. The disciples fall on their faces, terrified. And then the gentlest moment. Jesus comes and touches them: "Arise, and be not afraid." They look up, and there's no one but Jesus. Then they walk back down the mountain, and waiting at the bottom is a crowd, and a father with a sick boy. The light doesn't last. Life resumes. Orthodox Christians treasure this story deeply, and speak of the light on the mountain as God's own light, which the saints can come to share. Many churches keep the feast on August sixth.
screen: `METAMORPHOSIS: CHANGED IN FORM.` · `MOSES AND ELIJAH APPEAR.` · `LET US MAKE THREE TENTS.` · `BACK DOWN TO THE CROWD.` · then, large: `HIS FACE DID SHINE AS THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and close your eyes if you like. Go looking for one moment of pure light in your own life. It doesn't have to be religious. A morning, a face, a song, a place, a silence. Bring it back as clearly as you can: the light, the sound, the air. Stay with it. Let it warm you. Then, gently, let it go, and notice that you're still carrying something of it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Transfiguration. From the Latin, and behind it the Greek for metamorphosis: changed in form. On a mountain his face shone like the sun.
Your line: you can't stay on the mountain. Today, remember your moment of light, and then take some of it down to someone who needs it. Day fifty-eight.

what it means: three friends see him shining, want to stay forever, and are sent back down the mountain to a crowd.
what a scholar hears: metamorphoo is the root of metamorphosis, and Orthodox teachers speak of this light as God's own uncreated light, which the saints can come to share.

59.title: Zacchaeus up a tree (Luke 19:1–10)
59.hook: a short, hated tax collector climbs a sycamore; Jesus invites himself for dinner
59.howItsDone: Many churches read the story of Zacchaeus at the dedication of a church building, and it's a favorite in children's Sunday school, often with a song. Christians often point to it when speaking of restitution: making amends in practical ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, transfiguration: a face like the sun, and Peter wanting to build tents. Your line was you can't stay on the mountain. Who did you carry the light to? Now the road runs south, through Jericho. Day fifty-nine.

Remember being the short kid at a parade, or at the back of a concert, bouncing on your toes and seeing nothing but shoulders? Now picture Jericho, an old city on the road up to Jerusalem. Jesus is passing through, and the streets are packed. One man wants very badly to see him. His name is Zacchaeus. Luke says he's the chief of the tax collectors, and rich, the kind of rich people knew came out of their own pockets. Nobody's going to make room for him. And he's short. So a grown, wealthy, powerful, unpopular man runs ahead and does something undignified. Today, Zacchaeus up a tree.
screen: `BOUNCING ON YOUR TOES.` → `A CROWD IN JERICHO.` → `A SHORT, RICH, HATED MAN.`

segments.voice: Luke says he "climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way." A sycamore fig, a wide, low tree with branches easy to climb, not the American sycamore. There he is, a rich official, sitting in a tree like a boy. And Jesus reaches the spot, stops, looks up, and says his name: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Nobody has told Jesus his name. And he doesn't wait for an invitation. He invites himself to dinner. Zacchaeus scrambles down and welcomes him joyfully. But the crowd grumbles, all of them, Luke says: "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." And then, before anyone asks him to, Zacchaeus stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Fourfold. The law of Moses asked a thief to pay back four sheep for one stolen sheep. Zacchaeus holds himself to the thief's standard, on his own. Notice the order. Jesus didn't say, change first, then I'll come. He called him by name, came to his house, and the change came after, freely. Then Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house," and gives the line that sums up Luke's Gospel: "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." And a small irony. The name Zacchaeus comes from a Hebrew word meaning pure, or innocent. The whole town called him a sinner. Jesus called him by his name.
screen: `UP A SYCAMORE FIG.` · `ZACCHAEUS, MAKE HASTE, AND COME DOWN.` · `THE CROWD GRUMBLES.` · `HALF TO THE POOR, FOURFOLD BACK.` · then, large: `TO SEEK AND TO SAVE THAT WHICH WAS LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of one thing you got wrong with someone. Not the worst thing you ever did. Something you could actually fix. Money you owe. A promise you broke. Credit you took that wasn't yours. A harsh word you never took back. Picture the person. Now picture what making it right would look like. Maybe a message, a payment, an apology, a phone call. Don't beat yourself up. Zacchaeus didn't. He just stood up and said what he'd do. If you pray, you can ask for the courage. The bell holds the time.
Zacchaeus up a tree. A short, rich, hated man in a sycamore fig, called down by name, who gives half away and pays back four times over.
Your line: he knows your name. Today, make one thing right that you got wrong. Start small, but start. Day fifty-nine.
